description:
Vita Sallas

Our brazilian team is made up of people who are passionate about technology, space exploration, innovation, and web development. Our goal is to use programming and creativity to transform ideas into digital solutions that contribute to solving the challenges proposed by NASA. We are interested in creating modern, intuitive, responsive, and accessible websites that present scientific information in a clear, interactive, and engaging way.

We aim to develop our skills in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, interface design, data organization, and teamwork. We believe that bringing together different skills, perspectives, and ideas is essential to creating high-quality projects and overcoming complex challenges.

Joining our team is an opportunity to gain hands-on experience, share knowledge, develop new skills, and collaborate on a project with a scientific and technological purpose. We value creativity, communication, commitment, curiosity, and a willingness to learn, regardless of each participant's level of experience.
summary:
We are the Vita Sallas team, responsible for developing a program focused on the health and well-being of astronauts during space missions.

Our main goal is to develop a system that monitors astronauts' physical and environmental conditions, helping identify possible changes and contributing to their safety and quality of life throughout space missions.

Our website works as a space health monitoring center. It brings together different tools, such as heart rate, oxygen levels, body temperature, and radiation monitoring. It also offers an interactive map of the human body, physiological indicator analysis, crew report registration, a virtual assistant, and educational games. In addition, it provides official NASA videos to expand knowledge about health in space.

Therefore, Vita Sallas represents our proposal to combine technology, innovation, and healthcare, contributing to astronauts' safety and well-being during space missions, as well as helping prevent potential health problems.
details:
Vita Sallas is a web-based prototype of an integrated space health platform. It starts from a simple observation: during a space mission, the information that matters for a crew member’s well-being comes in very different forms (physiological readings, environmental conditions, symptom observations, written crew reports, medical documents) and serves very different needs (monitoring, record keeping, learning and day-to-day support). In most tools these live apart. Vita Sallas brings them into a single interface, so that monitoring, records, education, assistance and even light entertainment sit in one place. It is important to say from the outset what the project is not: it is a functional demonstration of a technological proposal, not a medical device, not a diagnostic tool, and not connected to any real spacecraft, mission control center or physician. It is designed to support, never replace, health professionals and official mission protocols.

1. What the project does and how it works

The platform is organized as a single dashboard presented as a space health command interface. At the top sits Vita Watch, a monitoring panel that displays three readings: heart rate (bpm), oxygen level (%) and body temperature (°C). Before the watch is “connected” these fields are empty. Once the user selects Connect Watch, the values are produced by a built-in simulator, and the interface states explicitly that they do not come from a real device. Alongside the watch, an overall status panel and summary cards for heart rate, oxygen level, radiation and body temperature give a quick view of the session’s condition, starting from an “awaiting data” state until information is provided. The environmental side of the platform is built around a mission location selector with six options: Earth surface, low Earth orbit, the International Space Station, the lunar surface, the Martian surface and interplanetary transit. Choosing a destination automatically fills a set of environmental fields: radiation, relative gravity, distance from Earth, air quality, cabin temperature and days in confinement. These values are fictional presets used for demonstration, and the platform labels them that way. The user can then run an environment analysis. In parallel, a physiological indicators form lets the user enter heart rate, oxygen saturation and body temperature and run an indicator analysis, and a trends chart plots the latest assessments of the session so that changes in the recorded values can be seen over time. Page 1 of 10Vita Sallas: Detailed Project Description The record-keeping layer is where the platform becomes more than a dashboard. An interactive body map lets the user select a body region and register a sign or symptom (pain, swelling, tingling, weakness, discomfort, no symptoms or other), a perceived intensity from 0 to 10, and free-text notes; records are saved per area and can be reviewed later. A crew report form accepts written observations, with optional voice dictation. A medical report form accepts image files (PNG, JPG, WEBP or DICOM) together with a chosen recipient and an optional note, and a camera function allows images to be captured through the browser and uploaded to the prototype. A “Mission Control Transmission” function then bundles indicators, environmental data, body records, crew reports, watch readings and uploaded files into one package. In this prototype that package is stored only on the application’s own server; it illustrates the idea of a consolidated health package without sending anything to a real mission team. The Vita Assistant acts on top of these records. When the user selects the option to analyze all records, the assistant reviews the indicators, environmental data, body records and submitted crew reports, and responds with orientation based on illustrative ranges. It also offers quick access to topics such as sleep, isolation and environment. Its responses are explicitly illustrative and are not a professional assessment. Finally, an educational layer is built into the same page. Health games in three formats (a decision challenge, a myth-or-fact quiz and a mission checklist) teach users to recognize warning signs and choose safe responses, with a session score for engagement. A learning hub gathers six official NASA videos, linked from their original NASA sources, covering exercise on the International Space Station, sleep and team dynamics, health risks such as radiation and microgravity, self-care and leisure, food, and sleeping aboard the station, together with links to the NASA Human Research Program video gallery and NASA eClips. The games are labeled as educational and as not replacing official training, mission protocols or the medical team. The features are designed to complement each other. The monitoring panels and forms create the data; the environment selector gives that data context; the body map, crew report and medical report preserve what the numbers cannot express; the assistant helps the user look at all of this together; and the games and NASA videos explain why these factors matter. A symptom recorded on the body map, a reading that departs from the expected range and a demanding environmental condition, such as a long period of confinement, can be reviewed in the same place instead of in three disconnected tools.

2. Benefits

The prototype already demonstrates several concrete benefits at the level of concept and interface. It centralizes health-related and environmental information that would otherwise be scattered. It organizes physiological indicators in a structured way and shows how recent assessments change within a session. It makes it easy to register crew observations, body-region symptoms and medical files in a consistent format. It brings educational material, including official NASA content, into the same environment where the data is handled, and its games turn learning about warning signs into an interactive activity. It also keeps the limitations visible, with simulation notices on the main functions, which supports honest use of the tool. Other benefits are possibilities for future development and should not be read as implemented capabilities. With real sensors, a validated data pipeline and review by medical professionals, a platform of this kind could help crews notice changes in their own data sooner, give mission teams better organized information to review, and contribute to safety, quality of life and well-being during long missions. None of this is claimed for the current prototype, which cannot prevent medical problems, produce accurate diagnoses or replace any health professional.

3. Intended impact The impact we hope to achieve is twofold. In the near term, the project aims to raise awareness and understanding of the physical and environmental challenges astronauts face, including radiation, altered gravity, distance from Earth, confinement and isolation, and to show in an accessible way that health in space involves the body, the environment and the mind together. The educational content and games serve this directly, and they are useful for students, space enthusiasts and anyone learning about spaceflight. In the longer term, the project proposes a direction: a single, organized and approachable environment in which crew members and medical teams could keep track of health information, observations and learning resources. Realizing that direction would require physical sensors, secure integration with external systems, and clinical and operational validation, all outside the scope of this prototype. The impact we claim today is therefore that of a demonstrated concept that makes the idea concrete, testable by others and open to improvement.

4. Tools, languages, hardware and software

The prototype was built with the following technologies, each with a defined role. HTML structures the content and elements of the interface. CSS provides the styling, visual organization and responsive presentation. JavaScript implements the client-side interactions, such as the simulated watch behavior, the body map, forms, analyses, charts and games. Python with the Flask framework provides the server-side application structure and ties the platform’s features together, including receiving the reports and Page files that the prototype stores. GitHub was used to host the source code, and Render was used to host the deployed website. Together, the browser-side layer delivers the experience and the server-side layer organizes and stores the records. ChatGPT was used as an artificial intelligence tool during development, mainly to help identify, correct and resolve bugs. It was a development aid and is not a component of the platform that the user sees. In the interest of accuracy, this description does not claim the use of physical sensors, wearable devices, other hardware, external APIs or a dedicated database. The Vita Watch values are generated by a simulator, the environmental values are fictional presets and not NASA telemetry, and the NASA resources used are the official educational videos linked from their original sources.

5. Creativity and innovation

A conventional informational page explains a subject. Vita Sallas lets the user work inside one. Its distinguishing idea is not any single feature, since a heart rate display or a set of educational videos is not novel in itself. The contribution is the integration, in one environment, of simulated monitoring, environmental context, organized records, an interactive body map, a virtual assistant, educational games and official NASA material, with the assistant reading across the data rather than looking at one field at a time. Treating monitoring, records, education, assistance and entertainment as parts of the same experience reflects the view that well-being in space is not only a matter of numbers: sleep, isolation and morale appear alongside physiology in both the assistant’s topics and the learning content. The interactive body map turns a symptom into a record that is easy to locate, rate and annotate, and the games turn passive reading into practice in recognizing warning signs. Together they make learning and tracking more accessible, organized and engaging than static material. The design also has room to grow. Possible directions include connecting real wearable sensors, adding validated reference ranges developed with medical professionals, supporting secure communication with real teams, and extending the learning content. These are opportunities for future work and are not part of the present prototype.

6. Factors and needs considered

The proposal reflects several needs that are specific to the space environment. Spaceflight can produce physiological changes, which is why the platform tracks heart rate, oxygen level and body temperature and gives space to body-region symptoms. Radiation and other environmental factors affect crews, so radiation, relative gravity, distance from Earth, air quality and cabin temperature are part of the environmental picture. Confinement and isolation affect behavior, sleep and team dynamics, which is why days in confinement appear among the environmental fields and why the assistant offers topics on sleep and isolation and the learning hub includes NASA content on sleep and team dynamics. Because health information comes in different natures (numbers, symptoms, text, images and documents), the platform was shaped around bringing them together in an organized way. Ease of use also guided the interface: a single page, clear labels, guided forms and visible simulation notices. As for how much was verified, these factors are what can be identified in the proposal and in the prototype’s design. This description does not claim that the team carried out user studies, clinical validation, expert consultation or formal testing, and none should be assumed. One constraint is confirmed: the prototype was developed within the limits of a hackathon, which shaped the choice of web technologies, simulated data and local storage over hardware integration.

7. Technical transparency and limitations

Vita Sallas should be understood as a functional demonstration prototype. The Vita Watch readings are simulated and do not come from a connected physical watch. The environmental data used in the demonstrations are fictional. Records and files are stored in the application’s own environment and are not transmitted to NASA, to the International Space Station or to any medical team, and the recipient options only record an intended routing choice. The virtual assistant uses illustrative parameters and does not replace professional assessment. The prototype has no capability for real medical monitoring, clinical diagnosis or operational integration with space systems. Several things would be needed to move beyond this stage, and they depend on parts that are physical, external to our proposal and potentially costly: real sensors and wearable devices, integration with external systems and secure communication, and rigorous validation with medical and aerospace specialists. We state this openly because we believe the project’s value lies in an organized, accessible concept that others can evaluate, and not in claims the prototype cannot support.
